source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (Computational Brain and Behavior; preprint read), reconstructed from the Luchins (1942) thesis
finding: Luchins' design: one warm-up problem, five E-problems all solved by B - A - 2C, then critical problems C1/C2 (solvable by the E method or a shorter A - C or A + C method), an extinction problem (only the short method works), then C3/C4. The control group skipped the E-problems. The plain trained group kept using the long E-solution; the control group never did.
numbers: Experiment 1: 310 subjects (NYU students and New York school pupils), 155 plain and 155 control. E-solution on C1/C2: 128 of 155 (83%) plain vs 0 of 155 control. On C3/C4: 100 of 155 (65%) plain vs 0 control. Plain C1/C2 vs C3/C4: 83% vs 65%, chi2=13.0, p<.001.
limits: Pen-and-paper, group-tested, population-level tables only; no reaction times or individual data. Numbers re-coded by the authors from percentages in the thesis tables.
agent_relevance: Founding effect is near total: trained 83% long method, untrained 0%. A history of success with one method gives a very large choice shift on problems where it still works but is wasteful. This is the G1/S6 target: a working method that is not the best one.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (Computational Brain and Behavior; preprint read) - Don't be blind condition
finding: In the Don't be blind (DBB) condition, subjects were told in advance to write the words 'Don't be blind!' after problem six. This cut the long method but did not remove it.
numbers: DBB group n=153. E-solution on C1/C2: 87 of 153 (57%) vs plain 83% (chi2=24.16, p<.001). On C3/C4: 57 of 153 (37%) vs plain 65%. So 43% (C1/C2) and 63% (C3/C4) used the short method.
quote: After you will have completed Problem Six, write on your papers the words Don't be blind!
limits: The summary claim 'over half switched' holds only for C3/C4 (63%), not C1/C2 (43%). The warning was a one-off cue, not a procedure. The authors model it as a higher inverse temperature (more effort per decision).
agent_relevance: A short warning helps but does not cure: expect a partial effect (about 25 points drop in long-method use). Our test (b) should expect partial gain, and a warning may work on a model only if it changes how much search is done, not just the wording.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (Computational Brain and Behavior; preprint read) - number of training problems
finding: More training problems made the set stronger. Ten E-problems gave almost no short-method use; two E-problems gave a smaller effect.
numbers: Luchins thesis tables 12-13: ten E-problems, 112 subjects: 112 of 112 (100%) used E on C1/C2 and 111 of 112 (99%) on C3/C4. Two E-problems, 108 subjects: 79 of 108 (73%) on C1/C2 and 59 of 108 (55%) on C3/C4. chi2=34.64 and 61.93, both p<.001.
limits: Contradicts Luchins' own text claim that number beyond a few does not matter; the reconstructed tables show a clear dose effect. Between-group, not randomized in a modern sense.
agent_relevance: The dose of repeated success matters. In an agent, many earlier successful steps with one tactic in context (long history, many few-shot examples of one route) may raise lock-in; a reset or summary of history may help (S6 operator choice).

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (Computational Brain and Behavior; preprint read) - interleaving D-problems in training
finding: If training alternated E-problems and D-problems (where the short method is the best), the set mostly disappeared.
numbers: Luchins thesis tables 14-15: alternating group 20 of 124 (16%) used E on C1/C2 vs plain group 97 of 121 (80%); chi2=100.65, p<.001. Seven training problems; college students at New York universities.
limits: Reconstructed from tables; not randomized in the modern sense.
agent_relevance: Mixed experience with more than one route type is the strongest cheap guard in the founding data (stronger than the warning). Supports showing or generating more than one route type before settling (G1 trigger, S4 harvest of dropped candidates).

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (Computational Brain and Behavior; preprint read) - time pressure
finding: Telling subjects they were being timed (large clock, three stopwatches) made the set stronger.
numbers: Plain group 153, speedy group 98. E on C1/C2: 126 of 153 (82%) plain vs 95 of 98 (97%) speedy, chi2=12.08, p<.001. On C3/C4: speedy 94 of 98 (96%) vs plain 100 of 153 (65%), chi2=31.8, p<.001.
limits: The preprint prints plain C3/C4 as 0.55 in one place and 100 of 153 (0.65) in the counts; treat it as 0.55 to 0.65. Also 'speedy' C3/C4 printed 0.99 vs count 94 of 98.
agent_relevance: Pressure to answer fast raises lock-in, so tight token or time budgets may raise the trap rate. Test trap rate by budget arm.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (Computational Brain and Behavior; preprint read) - age and intelligence
finding: Luchins did not find a strong effect of general intelligence or education on the size of the effect. Later work by Luchins and Luchins (1959) and Ross (1952) found the effect grew with age, even with IQ controlled. The authors re-split Luchins' data into four age groups.
numbers: 504 subjects across primary school, junior high, senior high and college freshmen in the thesis data. (Per-group percentages are in the paper's figure; not recorded here.)
limits: IQ null is from Luchins' reports as summarised by the authors, not a re-analysis. The age trend came later, in the 1950s.
agent_relevance: 'IQ unrelated' is supported only as a null in the founding studies. Do not expect a smarter or larger model to be immune; the later chess and LLM data point the same way.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (Computational Brain and Behavior; preprint read) - resource-rational model
finding: A formal model: the solver has a prior over solutions (learned from earlier problems) and picks a posterior policy that maximises expected utility minus a KL cost of moving away from the prior, with inverse temperature beta. The utility favours valid and also simple solutions.
numbers: Hand-tuned to Luchins' conditions: beta=25, learning rate 0.5 for plain: E-solution in 90 of 100 simulated agents on C1/C2 and 84 of 100 on C3/C4; DBB (beta=30) 68 and 46 of 100; speedy (beta=15) 97 and 98 of 100; alternating training 23 of 100 vs 90 of 100 for E-only training.
limits: Preprint; parameters set by the authors, not fitted by likelihood; only the water-jar domain. Ablations show the KL cost, the adaptive prior and the simplicity term are all needed.
agent_relevance: A formal reading of why the effect is rational under a compute limit. The fix is either more compute per decision (higher beta) or a less peaked prior (interleaving). Design handle: spend more search exactly when a familiar method fires (G1), not always.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology) - Luchins background as cited
finding: The paper restates Luchins' numbers: after five introductory problems over 80% of subjects used the long method on two critical problems, and 64% of the trained group failed the extinction problem against 5% of a control group.
numbers: Cited from Luchins and Luchins (1959): 64% failed the extinction problem after training vs 5% of controls who started with the critical problems.
limits: Second-hand figures. The extinction time limit was 2.5 min (per Thomas, Didierjean and Kuhn), so part of the failure is time-out from retesting the old method.
agent_relevance: The extinction problem is the cleanest agent test: the familiar method is certain to fail and the agent must drop it. Measure how many tries it wastes on a method that cannot work.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology) - Saariluoma (1990) chess replication, as cited
finding: Saariluoma (1990) used the water-jug design in chess: four smothered-mate training problems, then a problem with shorter solutions. 10 of 12 players missed the shorter ones. In a matched-group design only 11% of choices were optimal when the familiar solution was present (67% went to the familiar one); 69% found the optimal one when the familiar solution was disabled.
numbers: Experiment 2: 12 players, 10 missed shorter solutions. Experiment 3: two groups of 6; 11% optimal and 67% familiar vs 69% optimal when the familiar solution was disabled by moving one piece.
limits: Reported through Bilalic et al.; tiny groups; the 1990 original was not opened.
agent_relevance: Shows the block is caused by the familiar solution being present, not by the optimal one being hard. This is the control design our test should copy: the same problem with and without the familiar route.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology) - Experiment 1
finding: Chess players had to find the shortest mate in a position with a familiar five-move smothered mate and a shorter three-move mate (2-solution problem). The control version had only the short mate (1-solution). The familiar solution cut expert success to the level of players about 3 SD weaker.
numbers: 2-solution problem found by: Grand Masters 100% (n=6), International Masters 50% (n=6), Masters 18% (n=11), Candidate Masters 0% (n=11). 1-solution problem: all four expert groups 100%; Class A (n=8) 63%, Class B (n=8) 13%, Class C (n=8) 0%. Logistic regression B=.013 per Elo point; 100 Elo points cut the odds by a factor of 3.67.
quote: the more expert they were, the less prone they were to the effect
limits: Table layout is garbled in the extracted text; values read from the prose, which match: IM 50% vs Class A 63%, Master 18% vs Class B 13%, CM 0% vs Class C 0%. One problem only.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the cost: an expert is reduced to the level of a player 3 SD weaker by one tempting route. For an agent, the trap can cost the equivalent of a much smaller model.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology) - Experiment 2
finding: Five problem pairs (2-solution vs 1-solution). The effect replicated in graded form and was smaller for stronger players. One easy problem (number 5) showed no effect.
numbers: Success on 2-solution problems: Grand/International Masters 92% (n=12), Masters 69% (n=12), Candidate Masters 35% (n=12). Weaker players on 1-solution problems: Class A 91%, Class B 66%, Class C 47%. Players who found the optimum averaged Elo 2357 vs 2242 for those who did not (t(34)=2.09, p=.044).
limits: Twelve experts predicted much higher success (97%, 89%, 73% for the three groups): experts were badly calibrated about the trap.
agent_relevance: Same pattern of poor self-prediction: judges cannot forecast their own lock-in. Do not use the agent's own claim that it checked alternatives as a signal (G2, G5).

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology) - Experiment 3 and theory
finding: Specialists in a chess opening line saw a three-problem sequence in which a plan fits problems one and two but not three. Stronger players avoided the plan. The authors explain this by chunks and templates: strong players have finer-grained chunks, so the familiar route is checked against small details.
numbers: 12 players (Grand Masters n=5, Masters n=4, Candidate Masters n=3). Players who found the right solution had median Elo 2547 vs 2258 for those who did not; U=2, p=.017.
limits: Small n. The finer-detail explanation is a theory; only partly tested by the eye-movement study that followed.
agent_relevance: Expertise cuts the effect when knowledge is fine-grained and sensitive to the small difference that breaks the familiar method. This argues for a check that targets the key difference (a mutated input), consistent with G3.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones (Cognition) - Experiment 1 (eye movements)
finding: Candidate Masters with eye tracking. Players in the 2-solution problem all said the smothered mate was the shortest and said they were looking for something shorter. But their gaze stayed on the squares of the familiar solution the whole time.
numbers: Time to settle for smothered mate 37 s (SD 20). In the 1-solution problem players found the optimum in 79 s (SD 25). Familiar-solution group, squares by time period interaction: F(5,20)=0.6, ns (no gaze shift). 1-solution group: F(5,20)=11.9, p<.001, partial eta2=.75 (gaze moved gradually to the optimal squares). The same Einstellung players later found the optimum in the 1-solution problem (148 s, SD 90) with a gaze shift, F(5,20)=5.4, p<.001.
quote: they continued to look at features of the problem related to the solution they had already thought of
limits: Two small groups (df imply 5 per group); one position pair; Candidate Masters only.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that stated search for alternatives is not real search: people say 'I looked for better' while attention stays on the first idea. The same may hold for LLM visible reasoning (schema: reasoning text is not a reliable record). Code must force a different anchor.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones (Cognition) - Experiment 2
finding: Candidate Masters who saw only the 1-solution problem found the optimum in about half the time of players who had earlier failed the 2-solution problem and then saw the same 1-solution problem. The block lingers after the lure is removed.
numbers: Solution time about half; t(44)=2.16, p=.036, d=.65. Skill by group interaction F(2,40)=0.9, p>.40.
quote: Like a decaying priming effect, it continued to distract the players.
limits: Compares against the group from the 2008 Cognitive Psychology Experiment 1, so the groups were not randomized together.
agent_relevance: A failed attempt with the lure in context slows even a later clean attempt. This argues for restart in a fresh context after an impasse, not continued thinking in the same context.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2010) The Mechanism of the Einstellung (Set) Effect: A Pervasive Source of Cognitive Bias (Current Directions in Psychological Science)
finding: Review of the chess work and its general mechanism: once a problem is recognised as familiar, the matching schema is activated and steers attention, so information consistent with it is picked up and the rest is discarded. Linked to confirmation bias, negative transfer and part-set cueing.
numbers: Restates the Experiment 1 table: IM 50% on 2-solution vs Class A 63% on 1-solution; Master 18% vs Class B 13%; Candidate Master 0% vs Class C 0%. Easier problems show the effect in weaker players, harder problems in stronger ones.
limits: Review; the schema-guides-attention account is a mechanism claim backed by one eye-tracking pair.
agent_relevance: The mechanism claim is the best supported: first recognition biases what is looked at next. For our scaffold, the thing that matters is what the first answer makes the agent attend to, so S4 harvest should reset attention, not only list alternatives.

source: Sheridan and Reingold (2013) The Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions of the Einstellung Effect in Chess: Evidence from Eye Movements (PLoS ONE)
finding: Eye tracking of experts and novices on four chess problems, each with a familiar (Einstellung) move and a different optimal move. When the familiar move was good but suboptimal, players who chose it kept looking at it all trial; experts who found the optimal move gradually looked away. When the familiar move was a blunder, all experts and most novices avoided it and looked away.
numbers: 34 players (17 experts, 17 novices); 4 experimental plus 8 filler problems; 3-minute limit (reached on 10% of novice trials, 0% of expert trials). Move quality by problem type: expert ratings t(32)=6.04, p<.001; engine scores t(32)=4.93, p<.001. Gaze disengagement linear trend for experts F(1,66)=13.12, p<.01, not for novices F(1,66)=2.25, p=.138.
limits: Boundary condition: the effect needs the familiar solution to be acceptable. A visibly bad familiar move does not block.
agent_relevance: For our tests the lure must be a working but worse solution. If the lure visibly fails, a check kills it and no trap occurs (G2/G3 cover that); the dangerous lure is the one that passes the check.

source: Ellis and Reingold (2014) The Einstellung effect in anagram problem solving: evidence from eye movements (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Anagram version: six letters, a central three-letter string that is part of the answer, three loose letters, find the five-letter word. A familiar word as the central string slowed solving compared with a non-word, but the eyes showed both help and harm: shorter looks at the word string, longer looks at the loose letters.
numbers: 60 undergraduates. Accuracy 51.7% (word) vs 53.8% (non-word), t(59)=1.52, ns. Response time 15.3 s (word) vs 13.4 s (non-word), t(59)=3.25, p<.01. Dwells on central string 8.11 vs 6.76, t(59)=4.69, p<.001. Overall accuracy 52.7%, mean solve time 14.3 s.
limits: Here the effect is a slowdown, not an accuracy loss; familiarity also aids encoding, so the effect is mixed (interference plus facilitation).
agent_relevance: The cost of a familiar chunk can show up as time (more steps) rather than wrong answers. Measure steps and tokens to a correct answer, not only accuracy.

source: Thomas, Didierjean and Kuhn (manuscript) It is magic! How impossible solutions prevent the discovery of obvious ones
finding: A false solution that participants knew was impossible still inhibited finding the real, simple method of a magic trick. The block does not vanish when the lure is ruled out.
numbers: N=120 (40 per version). 82.5% proposed the false solution in the control. Real secret found by 60% in the false-solution-extinction version vs 87.5% without the false solution; chi2=7.81, p<.01. The paper states Luchins' extinction time limit was 2 min 30 s.
limits: Manuscript; magic trick task with a live performer; link to Luchins is by analogy. Earlier work (Thomas and Didierjean 2016) found that an unlikely, explicitly ruled-out false solution did not block.
agent_relevance: A lure refuted by evidence still costs discovery (27 points here). Refuting the first answer is not enough; the agent also needs a route that does not start from the refuted answer (S6).

source: Ninomiya, Iwata, Terai and Miwa (2024) Effect of cognitive load and working memory capacity on the efficiency of discovering better alternatives: a survival analysis (Memory and Cognition)
finding: Extended water-jar task with five jars and 62 trials (induction, set, up to 45 critical trials, inspection). Making the trained procedure more complex (higher load) made people find the shorter alternative sooner, in trials to discovery, while the share who found it at all did not differ.
numbers: Experiment 1: 74 Japanese university students (mean age 18.4). Survival curves differ, chi2(1)=4.97, p=.028; proportional hazards check chi2(1)=0.70, p=.402. Found the alternative at all: 25 (low complexity) vs 27 (high), Fisher p=.161. Experiment 2 (crowdsourced, split by working memory) found the effect strongest for high working memory capacity.
limits: Contradicts the simple idea that load always raises rigidity. The paper also notes that Luchins (1942) found more set responses under time pressure.
agent_relevance: Making repeated use of the old method costly helps the search for another; suggests a per-tactic budget as an operator for S6.

source: Crooks and McNeil (2009) Increased Practice with Set Problems Hinders Performance on the Water Jar Task (Cognitive Science Society proceedings)
finding: Six between-subject doses of set problems (0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 40). Flexibility fell with dose. This tests Luchins' claim that more than one set problem makes no difference and finds he was wrong. No U-shape in the range 0-40.
numbers: N=81 after exclusions (107 recruited; 16 excluded for knowing the task). Single-step use on both pre-extinction critical problems: 29% overall (24 of 81); by dose 0: 76%, 1: 22%, 5: 27%, 10: 0%, 20: 12%. Logistic beta=-0.15, z=-3.87, p<.001 (odds drop 1.16x per set problem). Extinction problem solved by 83% (67 of 81), beta=-0.089, p=.048. After extinction 54% used the single step on both.
limits: Small conditions (about 13 each); undergraduates; fatigue or boredom could explain part of the 40-problem result.
agent_relevance: A modern dose-response curve: most of the damage is there by 1 to 5 set problems and floors by 10. An agent may need only a few repeated successes for lock-in.

source: Lovett and Anderson (1995) Making heads or tails out of how people select problem-solving strategies (CogSci 1995, ACT-R)
finding: ACT-R model of strategy choice in the Building Sticks Task: each strategy is a production; choice goes to the strategy with the highest estimated chance of success (a Bayesian estimate from counts of successes and failures plus a prior) with Gaussian noise. History of success drives later choice, the production-system version of the Einstellung mechanism.
numbers: 68 CMU students (one removed for recalling Luchins' jars: 67 analysed), 90 problems, success ratios 80/20 and 60/40. Model fit R2=.99 on binned subject-problems and R2=.66 per subject on the last 45 problems. 6 of 48 subjects in three conditions picked the better strategy on at least 43 of the last 45 problems.
limits: Conference version; the journal paper (Lovett and Anderson 1996, Cognitive Psychology) was not opened. This page does not report a set-induced failure; it describes the choice model. Read through a summarising fetch.
agent_relevance: A small testable model: tactic choice follows counts of past success with that tactic. A program-side counter of how often a tactic has worked could be a lock-in signal (G1 trigger).

source: Alavi Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi and Taati (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Exploring Creative Problem Solving and Einstellung Effect with the OnlyConnect Wall Dataset (NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks)
finding: Early LLM test: Only Connect Wall puzzles with deliberate red herrings. GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 solve few walls fully. The authors also build variants with fewer red herrings and report higher scores there.
numbers: Test set 494 walls (1976 groups). Human reference: 285 of 494 walls, 1405 of 1976 groups. GPT-4 0-shot: 6 walls, 239 correct groups; 3-shot 272 groups; 5-shot 7 walls; 10-shot 3 walls, 249 groups. GPT-3.5-turbo 0-shot: 0 walls, 114 groups; 5-shot 2 walls, 149 groups.
limits: The link to Einstellung is by analogy to the fixation literature: there is no training sequence, and the lure is built into the puzzle. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 from early 2023 are old models. Numbers for the randomised variants were not recorded.
agent_relevance: An early finding that models are weak when the puzzle holds designed lures; few-shot helps a little and gets worse at 10 examples (more context did not help).

source: MedEinst authors (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs through Counterfactual Differential Diagnosis (arXiv 2601.06636)
finding: Benchmark of paired medical cases: a control case and a trap case where one discriminating piece of evidence flips the correct diagnosis. Bias Trap Rate is the share of control-correct pairs where the model still gives the control diagnosis on the trap case. Reported finding: stronger models do not escape; some have higher trap rates.
numbers: 5,383 paired cases, 49 diseases, 17 LLMs (built from DDXPlus). Reported in the arXiv HTML: GPT-5 baseline 54.30%, trap rate 51.87%; Gemini-2.5-Pro 53.58% and 60.90%; Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.09% and 42.98%; Qwen3-32B 40.25% and 43.46%. Their agent method on Qwen3-32B: baseline 69.49%, robust accuracy 24.21%, trap rate 33.75%.
limits: Page was read through a summarising fetch, not the PDF; one value differs by 0.01 inside the paper; the benchmark defines Einstellung itself and does not cite Luchins in the part read. Several results use models as judges. Treat numbers as indicative.
agent_relevance: A paired control/trap design we can copy: the same task with and without the changed key fact, trap rate defined only on pairs the model got right. Shows a bigger model can have a higher trap rate (G4: strength does not remove shared priors).

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology) - knowledge as set in other tasks, as cited (Wiley 1998; Frensch and Sternberg 1989)
finding: Two related findings cited by the paper: Wiley (1998) found that people with more baseball knowledge did worse on misleading remote-associates items where baseball suggested a wrong answer. Frensch and Sternberg (1989) found bridge experts adapted worse than novices to deep rule changes, though better overall.
numbers: No sample sizes given in the citing paper. Wiley: higher knowledge, lower score on misleading items only.
limits: Second-hand. The authors argue these show inflexibility only in a related domain, not true expert inflexibility, since the knowledge was not expertise in the test task.
agent_relevance: Prior knowledge in a lure's direction predicts worse results on lure items: in an LLM, strong domain knowledge may raise the pull of a wrong stock answer on trap items (Wiley-style test with matched control items).

source: Luchins (1942) Mechanization in problem solving: the effect of Einstellung (Psychological Monographs 54(6), Whole No. 248)
finding: The original monograph could not be opened here. Its content was read only through Binz and Schulz's table reconstruction (lines a01 to a07) and secondary summaries. Luchins' text claim that practice beyond one set problem does not matter is reported by Crooks and McNeil and is contradicted by the reconstructed tables.
numbers: Over 1000 subjects across conditions (as stated by Binz and Schulz).
limits: Not opened as a primary text. URL is the Crooks and McNeil page that cites it.
agent_relevance: Cite founding numbers to the reconstruction paper, not to the monograph.
